content: Orange juice is a liquid derived from the interior of an orange through methods such as squeezing, pressing, or crushing. Brazil is the largest exporter of orange juice, followed by the United States. On average, a single orange yields approximately 90 grams of juice. Freshly squeezed orange juice is characterized by its acidic citrus flavor, which is generally sweeter than the juice of lemons or limes. In addition to water and natural sugars, orange juice is an excellent source of vitamin C (ascorbic acid) and potassium. It is also a significant natural source of folic acid (vitamin B9), which is particularly recommended for women who are pregnant or planning to become pregnant. Citrus juices, including orange juice, contain flavonoids that are believed to confer various health benefits. However, consuming orange juice on an empty stomach can aggravate existing gastrointestinal conditions or cause mild, temporary stomach discomfort. Prolonged sipping of orange juice can also contribute to the erosion of tooth enamel due to its acidity. Commercial orange juice is often pasteurized in the United States to ensure safety and extend shelf life. Refrigerated orange juice sold to consumers may be labeled as not from concentrate. Some manufacturers enhance the juice by adding citric acid, ascorbic acid, or other nutrients such as calcium and vitamin D, which are not naturally present in oranges. Reduced-acid varieties of orange juice are also available for those who prefer a less acidic option. Frozen orange juice concentrate is produced by pasteurizing freshly squeezed and filtered orange juice, then evaporating most of the water under vacuum and heat before freezing. This process removes certain essences and oils, which are later reintroduced to restore flavor. The concentrated juice, typically at 65° Brix, is stored at approximately +10°F. To create frozen concentrate for sale, filtered water is added back to reduce the Brix level to 42° (about three times more concentrated than fresh juice). When water is added to reconstitute the thawed concentrate, it becomes ready-to-drink orange juice. Most orange juice sold globally today is reconstituted juice. Orange juice with pulp is considered more nutritious than pulp-free varieties due to the flavonoids present in the pulp. The price of orange juice varies significantly depending on whether it is sold as frozen concentrate or unprocessed juice. Futures contracts for frozen concentrated orange juice are traded on major commodity exchanges, such as the New York Board of Trade and the Brazilian Mercantile and Futures Exchange. Frozen concentrated orange juice (FCOJ) even played a central role in the 1983 movie Trading Places. Canned orange juice represents a small portion of the orange juice market. While canned juice retains vitamin C better than bottled juice, it tends to lose flavor if stored at room temperature for more than 12 weeks. Some producers add citric acid or ascorbic acid to orange juice to enhance its flavor or nutritional profile. Additionally, nutrients like calcium and vitamin D, which are not naturally found in oranges, may be added. Reduced-acid orange juice varieties are also marketed to cater to consumer preferences.
